lead.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old married White man, a high-school graduate in a professional specialty job in the private sector, born in the United States, working 40 hours a week with no capital gains or losses), the model predicts about {{C006.risk.from|pct}} chance of a low income ($50,000 or less).

The model adds up four parts: a long list of inputs that each push the prediction one way, a switch for large capital gains, a bend in age, and a group of small patches for a few occupations and countries of birth.

sentences.text: A higher education level lowers the predicted chance of a low income in stages: for a typical person, going from {{C059.statement.change.from}} (a typical 11th-grade leaver) to {{C059.statement.change.to}} (a typical bachelor's graduate) takes it from about {{C059.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C059.risk.to|pct}}, flattening out near the top because the predicted chance cannot go much higher.

Higher capital gains lower it steadily through this list (from about {{C060.risk.from|pct}} at {{C060.statement.change.from}} to about {{C060.risk.to|pct}} at {{C060.statement.change.to}} for a typical person, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower), and capital gains also act through the switch below; higher capital losses lower it steadily, from about {{C062.risk.from|pct}} at {{C062.statement.change.from}} to about {{C062.risk.to|pct}} at {{C062.statement.change.to}}.

Household and marriage raise it: a typical woman (so, as in the data, never married and not in a family) gets about {{C063.risk.to|pct}} rather than {{C063.risk.from|pct}}, a typical person who is not married (and so not in a family) about {{C065.risk.to|pct}}, and a typical own child rather than a husband about {{C067.risk.to|pct}}.
Being born in Ireland lowers it, from about {{C061.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C061.risk.to|pct}} for a typical person (the model has little data on this, n = {{C061.groups[1].n|d}}).

A second capital-gains part does nothing until about {{C103.shape.points_text.at}}, then lowers the predicted chance of a low income steadily: for a typical person, from about {{C103.risk.from|pct}} at {{C103.statement.change.from}} to about {{C103.risk.to|pct}} at {{C103.statement.change.to}} through this part.
It acts on {{C105.statement.n_active|d}} of {{C105.statement.n|d}} training people, and {{C105.statement.outcome_in_group.positives|d}} of them had a low income.

Being older lowers the predicted chance of a low income steadily up to about {{C107.shape.point.text}}, then no further: for a typical person, it goes from about {{C107.risk.from|pct}} at {{C107.statement.change.from}} to about {{C107.risk.to|pct}} at {{C107.statement.change.to}}, flattening out near the top because the predicted chance cannot go much higher.
A few occupations and countries of birth get a small extra push each, added together.

For a typical person, private household service raises the predicted chance of a low income from about {{C110.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C110.risk.to|pct}}, being born in China raises it to about {{C111.risk.to|pct}}, and handlers or cleaners raises it to about {{C112.risk.to|pct}}, while technical support lowers it to about {{C113.risk.to|pct}}.

A doctorate lowers the predicted chance a great deal, and even more so if the occupation is handlers or cleaners: for a typical person with a doctorate (and the education level such people have in the data), from about {{C119.risk.groups[0].from|pct}} to about {{C119.risk.groups[0].to|pct}} for handlers or cleaners, and from about {{C119.risk.groups[1].from|pct}} to about {{C119.risk.groups[1].to|pct}} in other occupations.
